notes.meaning: God gave this message to Jeremiah around 605 BC, during the fourth year of King Jehoiakim's rule over Judah. That was the same year the Babylonian army first invaded Jerusalem and carried off young captives. God chose this moment of danger to call His people to listen to Him.

God told Jeremiah to take a scroll made of animal skins or plant sheets and write down every message given to him over the last twenty-three years. Putting all these sermons together into one book would show the people the whole picture of God's truth. It also ensured that God's warnings would be preserved even if the prophet was silenced.

The Lord explained why He wanted His warnings written down: to offer Judah another chance to turn from sin. God did not desire to ruin them, but gave them every opportunity to repent and receive His full pardon. When people take God's warnings to heart, He gladly forgives their sins.

differ.view: God's foreknowledge is complete and His purposes never change; He spoke of 'perhaps' in human terms to show how stubborn the people were and to leave them without excuse.
God knew the people would refuse to repent, but He used this ordinary means of warning to show His justice and prove that their guilt was entirely their own.
God used the word 'perhaps' because His foreknowledge does not force human choices, leaving people with a genuine free will to accept or reject His mercy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The conditional warning shows that human free will must cooperate with God's grace, and hearing many prophecies together was designed to stir up genuine repentance.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah called for his faithful assistant Baruch, who was a skilled professional writer. The prophet spoke the words as God gave them to his memory, and Baruch carefully penned them all onto the scroll. God often pairs different people together so their skills can serve His kingdom.

Jeremiah told Baruch that he was barred from entering the temple grounds himself. While some think he was under guard, he was likely banned by temple authorities or warned away to keep him safe from royal anger. Even though the prophet was held back, God's message could not be stopped.

Jeremiah instructed Baruch to go to the temple during a public fast day to read the scroll out loud. A fast day was chosen because crowds of worshippers from towns all across Judah would be gathered in Jerusalem. Their hearts might also be more humble and open to God's message during a time of national trouble.

The goal of reading the warnings was to lead the people to fall on their faces in humble prayer. Outward fasting has no value unless people truly turn away from their evil deeds. God's anger against sin was severe, but sincere repentance would turn that anger away.

Baruch faithfully carried out every instruction Jeremiah gave him. Even though reading words of judgment to a crowd could have placed his life in danger, he did not hesitate to serve God. True faith shows itself in quiet, steady obedience.

In the winter of Jehoiakim's fifth year, about a year after God first commanded the scroll to be written, a special fast was called for the nation. This was not a regular yearly holiday, but an emergency gathering probably prompted by fear of the advancing Babylonian armies. The people themselves gathered to seek help from the Lord.

Baruch read the scroll from an upstairs room belonging to Gemariah, an official from a respected family that respected God. The room had a window or doorway opening onto the temple courtyard, allowing Baruch's voice to carry down to the crowd gathered below. God provided a safe and prominent place so all the people could hear.

Gemariah's son Micaiah was present in the temple court and listened closely to the words of the Lord. Recognizing that this message was of national importance, he decided it must be shared with the leaders of the land. When we hear God's truth, we should not keep it to ourselves.

Micaiah went down to the scribe's office in the royal palace, where the king's top advisors were holding an official meeting. The council included men from leading families, some of whom had shown support for God's prophets in the past. God had placed His words within reach of the highest leaders in the government.

Micaiah gave a full report of everything he had just heard Baruch read to the crowds at the temple. His report was so clear and serious that the officials recognized they needed to look into the matter immediately. A faithful witness can stir leaders to pay attention to God's warnings.

The council sent an officer named Jehudi to summon Baruch and bring the scroll to the palace. Baruch did not let fear hold him back, but went straight to the palace with the writings in his hand. God gives courage to His servants when they are called to stand before authorities.

The royal officials received Baruch politely, invited him to sit down, and asked him to read the scroll to them. Baruch read the entire message clearly, without backing down from the hard warnings it contained. God's messengers must deliver His words with patience and boldness.

As the officials heard the warnings of impending ruin, they looked at each other in deep alarm. They realized the threat was real, yet as royal counselors they were duty-bound to report such an important matter to the king. A good conscience is often pulled between fear of God and political duty.

The officials questioned Baruch carefully to find out the exact origin of the scroll. They wanted to know whether Baruch had written his own thoughts from memory or if Jeremiah had dictated each word directly to him. They were making sure of the facts before presenting the matter to the king.

Baruch answered plainly that Jeremiah had spoken every single word out loud, and that he had only recorded them in ink on the parchment. This proved that Jeremiah was inspired by God rather than reciting old notes, and that Baruch added nothing of his own. God's word comes through human voices, but its content belongs entirely to Him.

Knowing King Jehoiakim's violent temper and how he had executed another prophet earlier, the officials told Baruch that he and Jeremiah must hide in secret. They respected the men of God and wanted to protect them from the king's wrath. God can use sympathetic people in government to shield His servants.

The officials left the scroll secured in the secretary's office and went into the palace courtyard to speak with the king. They wisely kept the original scroll safe in case the king responded with fury. Prudence is a helpful partner to faith when facing dangerous rulers.

Jehoiakim would not settle for a summary, so he sent Jehudi to fetch the scroll and read it directly to him and his court. The king wanted to hear the exact words, though not out of a heart ready to repent. Curiosity about God's word is useless without a willing heart to obey it.

Because it was the cold winter season, the king was sitting in the winter wing of his palace by a portable metal pot of burning charcoal. The setting highlights the comfort and luxury of the royal court while the nation faced looming destruction. Earthly comforts can easily blind people to spiritual danger.

After Jehudi read just three or four columns of writing, the king took a scribe's knife, sliced those sections off, and tossed them into the fire pot until the whole scroll was burned. Jehoiakim acted deliberately, showing cold contempt for God's message. Destroying the paper that holds God's words can never stop His judgment from coming true.

Neither the king nor his personal attendants showed any fear or tore their clothes in sorrow as the holy words were consumed. In stark contrast, Jehoiakim's father Josiah had torn his clothes in deep grief when God's law was read to him years before. A hardened heart treats holy things with careless indifference.

Three of the officials bravely pleaded with Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll, but he refused to listen. These men showed courage by speaking up against a violent king to defend God's message. God remembers those who take a stand for truth even when they are overruled.

Jehoiakim ordered royal officers to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch, intending to silence them permanently. But the Lord kept them safe and hidden away so that the king's search parties could not find them. God is entirely capable of shielding His people when their enemies seek their lives.

After the scroll was reduced to ashes, the Lord spoke to Jeremiah again in his hiding place. The king had burned the parchment, but he had not silenced the living God who gave it. Human rebellion cannot stop the work of the Almighty.

God commanded Jeremiah to take a new scroll and write down every single word that had been on the first one. Just as the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments were remade after being broken, God restored His written revelation in full. God's truth outlasts all who try to destroy it.

The Lord told Jeremiah to record a specific verdict concerning King Jehoiakim. The king had objected to the warning that Babylon would conquer the land and leave it empty of people and animals. Rulers often hate God's word simply because it tells them truths they do not want to hear.

God decreed that Jehoiakim's royal line would lose the throne of David and that his corpse would be cast out without an honorable burial, left to bake in the day's heat and freeze in the night. The king who tossed God's scroll into the fire would himself be tossed outside the city walls. God's justice answers human pride with fitting dishonor.

differ.view: Jehoiakim's son reigned for only three months and his uncle was an illegitimate ruler, meaning the continuous direct line of David was broken until Christ came to reign forever.
Jehoiachin's three-month rule was so short and unrecognized by Babylon that it counted as nothing, leaving Jehoiakim without a true successor on David's throne.

notes.meaning: The Lord promised to bring upon Jehoiakim, his family, and all the people of Jerusalem every disaster He had warned them about. Because they repeatedly refused to listen to His gracious calls, judgment became unavoidable. Refusing God's mercy only makes His judgment certain.

Jeremiah gave a fresh scroll to Baruch, who wrote down all the original words again at the prophet's dictation, along with many new warnings. Opposing God's word never lessens His truth; it only brings greater judgment upon the rebel. In the end, God's written word was enlarged rather than destroyed.
